Honestly? No. I'd drop that thread.

Gender discrimination claims work by showing you were treated worse because of your sex. You're a man, the panel was men, and the person they hired was a man. There's no comparison to be drawn there. If anything, a panel that shared your demographic profile and still picked someone else cuts against the idea that identity drove the outcome. If you raised this in a grievance or complaint, it would land badly — it would read as grasping, and it would undercut the parts of your case that actually have substance.

There's one narrow exception: some municipalities have their own HR policies requiring diverse selection panels for senior appointments. If yours does and the panel breached it, that's a procedural non-compliance point — not evidence of bias against you, but a crack in the integrity of the process. Worth a look at the policy manual. Don't build on it, though; it's a footnote at best.

**What's actually worth your attention**

The silence on your written request is the real problem. Two weeks with no acknowledgement is poor practice, and in many jurisdictions there are formal routes that start ticking regardless of whether anyone replies to you — internal appeal or grievance windows, and access-to-information or freedom-of-information requests that can get you the scoring matrix, panel notes and the approved job description. Those deadlines are often short, sometimes 10 to 30 days from notification. Find out what applies where you are before anything expires.

**The credentials question is less of a slam dunk than it feels**

You have a master's, a licence and twelve years in. He has a bachelor's in geography. On paper that looks lopsided, and I understand why it stings. But "extensive experience of public consultation" is not filler language — for a planning director, it's frequently the hardest part of the job. Contentious rezonings, hostile public meetings, council members under pressure from constituents, developers pushing back. A panel that just watched its last director get chewed up in that arena will weight it heavily, and a master's degree doesn't speak to it at all.

So the question isn't whether you were more qualified in the abstract. It's whether the posting and the published criteria told you this was the dominant factor. If consultation experience wasn't in the posted requirements, or was listed as a minor "asset," and it then became the deciding criterion — that's a real procedural argument. If it was prominently in the posting and you didn't build your answers around it, the uncomfortable possibility is that you were out-interviewed.

**Two things I'd want to know**

Was the successful candidate an internal employee or otherwise known to the panel members? That's where unfair-process concerns usually actually live — not in panel demographics, but in whether someone was effectively pre-selected and the competition was decorative.

And how did the interviews feel in the moment? Did they probe public engagement, difficult council dynamics, handling angry residents? If they did and you leaned on technical planning expertise, that's useful information about what happened, even if it's not what you want to hear.

If you want, tell me your jurisdiction and I can be more specific about what records you can compel and what the deadlines look like.
